ocar.opportunity: Macroscale structural and functional connectomes now describe healthy organization, individual differences, and lifespan change, and they are being recruited to conceptualize brain disorders.
ocar.challenge: A shift toward high-level network models can sideline regional microstructure, local circuits, and non-imaging cellular, genetic, or chemical properties that actually constitute nodes and edges.
ocar.action: Larivière, Vos de Wael, Paquola, Hong, Mišić, Bernasconi, Bernasconi, Bonilha, and Bernhardt, in Brain Connectivity (2019), review how MRI tissue-microstructure markers, local function, and extra-imaging data can be integrated with large-scale connectome models.
ocar.resolution: They argue that enriching nodes and edges this way clarifies connection strength and better specifies the substrate of disorders in which local anomalies interact with network perturbations, including stroke, autism, and drug-resistant epilepsies. Conclusions highlight multivariate methods (canonical correlation, partial least squares) and connectome-informed in silico models of lesion consequences.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a program for microstructure-informed pathoconnectomics rather than a new reconstruction; prognostic use of lesion-effect models is cited as promising, not demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: Whole-brain wiring maps are useful, but they often treat regions as simple dots. This review argues that adding tissue texture and local cell biology to those maps would better explain healthy brains and diseases such as epilepsy, stroke, and autism.
summaries.intermediate: Larivière and colleagues (Brain Connectivity, 2019) review human MRI connectomics alongside meso- and microscale features: tissue-microstructure markers, local function, and cellular, genetic, or chemical data. Integrating those measures is presented as a way to define nodes and edge weights more realistically and to capture how focal anomalies interact with network-level change in stroke, autism, and drug-resistant epilepsy. The conclusions point to canonical correlation and partial least squares as formalisms for linking structural, functional, microstructural, and behavioral spaces, and to connectome-informed dynamical models as tools for lesion prognosis.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not an empirical connectome. Disease examples are illustrative. The selected extract’s conclusions run into acknowledgments, so multivariate and in silico claims are those stated there rather than a full methods comparison. No new numeric network statistics are reported.

plain_language_summary: Whole-brain wiring maps are useful, but they often treat regions as simple dots. This review argues that adding tissue texture and local cell biology to those maps would better explain healthy brains and diseases such as epilepsy, stroke, and autism.

ocar.opportunity: Stereotyped fly circuits are thought to be wired by cell-surface identity proteins. Two immunoglobulin superfamily groups, Dprs and DIPs, are strong candidates for synapse targeting.
ocar.challenge: How Dpr–DIP binding specificity is encoded in structure, and whether those interfaces can be engineered to probe particular circuits, was unknown.
ocar.action: Cheng, Ashley, Kurleto, Lobb-Rabe, Park, Carrillo, and Özkan, in eLife (2019), determine five crystal structures of Dpr–DIP and DIP–DIP complexes and use structure-guided mutations to retune specificity and affinity, testing engineered Dpr10 and DIP-α in the Drosophila neuromuscular circuit.
ocar.resolution: The structures show how gene duplication diversified recognition: distant duplications created specialized subclasses, whereas recent duplications largely yielded redundant interactions. Engineered receptors with novel specificities or modified affinities can be used to study circuits that require Dpr–DIP interactions, and both homophilic and heterophilic binding contribute to neuromuscular wiring.
ocar.future_work: The discussion calls for a comprehensive arthropod Dpr/DIP census to test whether receptor family expansion tracks neural-network complexity, and for matching connectomic and transcriptomic maps to accurate protein-interaction and structural data.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins to choose synaptic partners. This team solves several of those protein structures and redesigns them to show how the matches help wire a muscle circuit.
summaries.intermediate: Cheng and colleagues (eLife, 2019) report five crystal structures of Drosophila Dpr–DIP and DIP–DIP complexes and use them to engineer receptors with new specificities or affinities. They test engineered Dpr10 and DIP-α in the neuromuscular circuit and find roles for both homophilic and heterophilic binding. The discussion frames Dprs/DIPs as an arthropod-expanded toolkit whose older duplications specialized interactions while newer ones remain mostly redundant.
summaries.advanced: Five complexes are solved, not the full 21×11 Dpr–DIP matrix. Functional tests in this extract focus on one engineered pair in the neuromuscular system. Evolutionary claims about network complexity versus gene number are speculative. Connectomic matching is positioned as a future opportunity, not a result of this paper.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly neurons use matching surface proteins to choose synaptic partners. This team solves several of those protein structures and redesigns them to show how the matches help wire a muscle circuit.

ocar.opportunity: On–Off direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs) are a classic motion encoder, but their responses are also shaped by surrounding motion context.
ocar.challenge: The synaptic mechanisms of that contextual modulation, and whether On and Off pathways use the same motifs, were unknown.
ocar.action: Huang, Rangel, Briggman, and Wei, in Nature Communications (2019), combine synapse-specific genetics, patch clamp, and connectomic analysis in the mammalian retina to trace circuits that modulate posterior-preferring DSGCs (pDSGCs).
ocar.resolution: pDSGCs are sensitive to discontinuities of moving contours via contextually modulated cholinergic excitation from starburst amacrine cells. Distinct motifs upstream of On versus Off starbursts are required for bright versus dark contrasts. Wide-field amacrine cells with straight, unbranching dendrites act as “continuity detectors” of moving contours, extending DSGC encoding beyond direction selectivity.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s discussion is not captured (the tail is the reference list), so remaining experimental caveats and quantitative effect sizes should be read in the full paper.

summaries.beginner: Some retinal cells that report motion direction also notice whether a moving edge is continuous or broken. This study finds separate inner-retina circuits for bright and dark edges that create that extra sensitivity.
summaries.intermediate: Huang, Rangel, Briggman, and Wei (Nature Communications, 2019) show that posterior-preferring On–Off DSGCs are modulated by motion context through cholinergic excitation from starburst amacrine cells. Synapse-specific genetics, electrophysiology, and connectomics identify distinct upstream motifs for On versus Off pathways and a class of wide-field amacrine cells with unbranching dendrites that detect contour continuity. Divergent On/Off motifs therefore add discontinuity encoding on top of direction selectivity.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s discussion was not captured (tail is references and license text), so circuit claims follow the abstract and introduction. Species is mammalian retina (mouse methods are implied by the author list and typical DSGC genetics, but not named in the selected front matter). No numeric synapse counts or reconstruction volumes appear in the extract. Briggman’s role indicates EM connectomics, but volume size is not stated here.

plain_language_summary: Some retinal cells that report motion direction also notice whether a moving edge is continuous or broken. This study finds separate inner-retina circuits for bright and dark edges that create that extra sensitivity.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain simulators such as TheVirtualBrain need anatomically constrained connectomes; macaques can supply multi-scale data that rodents and humans do not jointly provide.
ocar.challenge: Existing tracer resources are incomplete or only categorically weighted, and diffusion tractography has well-known biases, so a usable macaque cortex-wide connectome for simulation is nontrivial to assemble.
ocar.action: Shen, Bezgin, Schirner, Ritter, Everling, and McIntosh, in Scientific Data (2019; catalog year 2018), combine axonal tract-tracing with macaque diffusion tractography to build a macaque (Macaca mulatta and M. fascicularis) connectome for whole-cortex TVB simulations, then simulate resting-state BOLD and fit it to empirical fMRI.
ocar.resolution: Best-fit simulated functional connectivity used G = 0.298 and sigma = 0.0255, with cosine similarity 0.75 versus empirical grand-average FC (greater than null networks, p < 0.001). PCA of simulated BOLD recovered frontal, superior-temporal/auditory, and visual networks. Individual-animal cosine similarities were 0.47–0.80 and were not significantly different when using each animal’s own connectome versus the canonical one (paired t-test p = 0.35); individual specificity instead appeared in biophysical parameters.
ocar.future_work: The extract flags limitations of probabilistic tractography. Canonical versus individual connectomes captured similar FC fits, so subject-specific structure is not shown to be required for this resting-state use case.

summaries.beginner: This team builds a macaque brain wiring map for a whole-brain simulator and shows that the simulated resting activity resembles real fMRI, including familiar frontal, auditory, and visual networks.
summaries.intermediate: Shen and colleagues (Scientific Data, 2019) construct a macaque cortical connectome for TheVirtualBrain by enhancing tract-tracing resources with diffusion tractography. Simulated resting-state BOLD best matched empirical FC at G = 0.298 and sigma = 0.0255 (cosine similarity 0.75; p < 0.001 versus nulls). Simulated networks resembled previously reported macaque resting-state systems; nodal strengths correlated with empirical FC (r = 0.51, p < 0.001). Fits to nine individual animals (cosine similarity 0.47–0.80) were similar with a canonical versus individualized connectome (p = 0.35), with more subject-specific parameter sets in the individualized case.
summaries.advanced: Catalog year is 2018; the PDF is the 2019 Scientific Data descriptor (received December 2018). Markov et al. coverage of 29 of 91 regions is cited as a limitation of an existing weighted tracer set, not as this paper’s parcellation size. Nine subjects appear in the individual-fit analysis; the extract does not state a single node count for the released connectome. Tractography limitations are acknowledged; cosine similarity is the reported fit metric, not Pearson r of full FC matrices except for nodal strength (r = 0.51).

plain_language_summary: This team builds a macaque brain wiring map for a whole-brain simulator and shows that the simulated resting activity resembles real fMRI, including familiar frontal, auditory, and visual networks.

ocar.opportunity: Serial histology sees cells but destroys 3D topology; reconstructing stacks, with or without 3D medical imaging as shape prior, can recover spatial relationships and link MRI contrast to microstructure.
ocar.challenge: Cutting, staining, and imaging introduce artefacts; realistic shape is hard without an independent 3D ground truth; and the problem spans histopathology, physics, computer vision, and medicine.
ocar.action: Pichat, Iglesias, Yousry, Ourselin, and Modat, in Medical Image Analysis (2018), survey almost three decades of methods for 3D reconstruction from serial sections, covering pipelines with and without 3D medical imaging, registration, validation, and applications.
ocar.resolution: They organize methods around recovering histology’s original topology, characterizing MRI signals from tissue, and building high-resolution anatomical atlases, and they stress that image registration is the workhorse for automated correspondence. Closing sections emphasize interdisciplinary workflow (histopathologist, physicist, computer scientist, physician) and remaining multimodal alignment challenges, including emerging CNN-based correspondence.
ocar.future_work: Trends flagged include better control of tissue alteration over time, ex vivo MRI interpretation after fixation or freezing, and learning-based multimodal registration; none is a new algorithm introduced here.

summaries.beginner: Slicing tissue for a microscope flattens a 3D object into a stack of 2D pictures. This review surveys decades of computer methods that restack those slices, sometimes using MRI as a shape guide.
summaries.intermediate: Pichat and colleagues (Medical Image Analysis, 2018) review nearly three decades of 3D histology reconstruction from serial sections, with and without 3D medical imaging. They summarize how specimens become digitized sections, the artefacts that follow, registration-based reconstruction, validation, and uses such as recovering topology and building atlases. The extract’s later discussion stresses cross-disciplinary coordination and remaining multimodal correspondence problems, including possible CNN approaches.
summaries.advanced: This is a survey (Medical Image Analysis 46:73–105), not a new reconstruction benchmark. The supplied PDF is a King’s College accepted manuscript with publisher portal front matter. Quantitative method rankings are not in the selected extract. “Almost three decades” is the authors’ scope statement.

plain_language_summary: Slicing tissue for a microscope flattens a 3D object into a stack of 2D pictures. This review surveys decades of computer methods that restack those slices, sometimes using MRI as a shape guide.

ocar.opportunity: Morphology skeletons from microscopy are used from visualization through simulation, so an integrated free toolkit could replace fragmented tracing-to-mesh pipelines.
ocar.challenge: Existing workflows are convoluted; tracing artifacts must be repaired before high-fidelity surface and volumetric models are usable for simulation or in silico imaging.
ocar.action: Abdellah, Hernando, Eilemann, Lapere, Antille, Markram, and Schürmann, in Bioinformatics (2018, ISMB), present NeuroMorphoVis, a Blender-based Python framework with C++/OpenMP volume tools, GUI and CLI, for building, visualizing, analyzing, and repairing neuronal morphology skeletons.
ocar.resolution: The software detects and repairs tracing artifacts and generates surface meshes and high-resolution volumetric models. Two case studies illustrate 3D soma profiles and volumetric circuit models for simulated in vitro imaging. Code is released at github.com/BlueBrain/NeuroMorphoVis under the GNU public license.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s later pages are references, so quantitative mesh-quality or timing benchmarks should be read in the full ISMB paper rather than inferred here.

summaries.beginner: Neuron tracings from microscopes often need cleanup before they can be turned into 3D models. This paper releases a free toolkit that repairs those tracings and builds meshes for visualization and simulation.
summaries.intermediate: Abdellah and colleagues (Bioinformatics/ISMB 2018) introduce NeuroMorphoVis, an interactive cross-platform framework (Blender Python API plus C++/OpenMP volume code) for neuronal morphology skeletons from microscopy. It repairs tracing artifacts and produces surface meshes and volumetric models. Applicability is shown in two case studies: 3D soma profiles and volumetric neuronal-circuit models for in silico imaging. Source and documentation are on GitHub under a GNU license.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s tail is the reference list, so case-study quantitative results are those in the abstract. This is a software/methods paper, not a new biological connectome. “High fidelity” and “high resolution” are authors’ descriptors, not measured error rates in this extract.

plain_language_summary: Neuron tracings from microscopes often need cleanup before they can be turned into 3D models. This paper releases a free toolkit that repairs those tracings and builds meshes for visualization and simulation.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has sex-shared neurons whose synapses are pruned or maintained in a sex-specific way, giving a cell-resolved model of sexually dimorphic connectivity.
ocar.challenge: The molecular signal that maintains male-specific synapses between the phasmid sensory neuron PHB and the sex-shared AVG interneuron was not known.
ocar.action: Weinberg, Berkseth, Zarkower, and Hobert, in Current Biology (2018), show that UNC-6/Netrin acting through UNC-40/DCC and CED-5/DOCK180 is required and sufficient for male-specific PHB>AVG maintenance, and they map the transcriptional logic of unc-6 in AVG.
ocar.resolution: unc-6 is transcribed in AVG in both sexes in juveniles, then downregulated in hermaphrodites at sexual maturation via TRA-1 antagonism of the LIM homeobox activator lin-11, while remaining on in males. Ectopic unc-6 in hermaphrodite AVG maintains PHB>AVG synapses. Intersectional transcriptional control of unc-6 is therefore necessary and sufficient to pattern this sexually dimorphic connection cell-autonomously.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s later pages are methods rather than a discussion of generality; whether the same Netrin logic patterns other dimorphic synapses is not established in this card.

summaries.beginner: Male and female roundworms keep different synapses between the same named cells. This study shows that a well-known guidance cue, Netrin, is left on in one male cell to preserve a male-specific connection.
summaries.intermediate: Weinberg, Berkseth, Zarkower, and Hobert (Current Biology, 2018) identify UNC-6/Netrin, UNC-40/DCC, and CED-5/DOCK180 as required and sufficient for male-specific maintenance of PHB>AVG synapses in C. elegans. Sex specificity comes from transcriptional downregulation of unc-6 in hermaphrodite AVG at maturation, via TRA-1 opposing lin-11. Ectopic unc-6 in hermaphrodites preserves the male-typical synapses. The PDF is an author manuscript (PMC 2019).
summaries.advanced: The extract’s tail is methods (smFISH, imaging), not a limitations section. Claims of cell-autonomous patterning follow the summary. Sufficiency is shown for this PHB>AVG pair via ectopic unc-6, not for the whole sexually dimorphic connectome. Catalog tags this as connectomics; the experiment is genetic and anatomical, not a new EM volume.

plain_language_summary: Male and female roundworms keep different synapses between the same named cells. This study shows that a well-known guidance cue, Netrin, is left on in one male cell to preserve a male-specific connection.

ocar.opportunity: Diffusion MRI histology could quantify whole-mouse-brain structural connectivity in disease models if scan time and spatial resolution were less tightly traded off.
ocar.challenge: Fully sampled high-resolution diffusion volumes are slow; accelerating acquisition must not destroy scalar metrics or graph measures of the connectome.
ocar.action: Wang, Anderson, Badea, Cofer, Dibb, Qi, and Johnson, in Brain Structure and Function (2018), apply compressed sensing to whole-mouse-brain diffusion MRI, reconstruct tensors, run DSI Studio tractography, and build connectomes with a 166-ROI atlas.
ocar.resolution: Compared with fully sampled data at the same scan time, compressed sensing at higher spatial resolution better visualized cortical layers, dentate gyrus, and cerebellum. Versus fully sampled data at the same resolution, FA and MD error stayed below 6.0% even at 8.0-fold acceleration, and node properties (strength, clustering coefficient, eigenvector centrality, local efficiency) correlated better than 95.0% with fully sampled connectomes. Color FA/DWI/MD at 45 μm isotropic CS were visually comparable to 90 μm fully sampled scans.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the acceleration as enabling routine application to mouse disease models; that application is prospective in this methods paper.

summaries.beginner: High-detail MRI of a whole mouse brain usually takes too long. This team uses compressed sensing so they can scan finer and still keep the wiring-map numbers close to a full slow scan.
summaries.intermediate: Wang and colleagues (Brain Structure and Function, 2018) accelerate whole-mouse-brain diffusion MRI with compressed sensing. At matched scan time, higher-resolution CS better showed cortical layers, dentate gyrus, and cerebellum. At matched resolution, FA and MD error remained <6.0% at 8.0× acceleration, and connectome node metrics correlated >95.0% with fully sampled graphs using a 166-ROI atlas (Calabrese et al. 2015). Figure 3 compares 90 μm fully sampled versus 45 μm CS tensors. The PDF is an author manuscript.
summaries.advanced: Error bounds (<6.0%, >95.0%) are those stated in the abstract; per-region maps are not in the extract. Tractography is DSI Studio with atlas priors, not EM. “Informed consent” boilerplate appears in the manuscript header despite an animal study. Angular sampling is 46 DWIs plus 5 B0 images in the illustrated protocol.

plain_language_summary: High-detail MRI of a whole mouse brain usually takes too long. This team uses compressed sensing so they can scan finer and still keep the wiring-map numbers close to a full slow scan.

ocar.opportunity: Neuron classes often split into subclasses that share many features but differ in select traits such as connectivity along the body axis.
ocar.challenge: Transcription factors that specify class identity were not clearly shown to also generate subclass diversity, and regional cues that could intersect with pan-class factors were incomplete.
ocar.action: Kratsios, Kerk, Catela, Liang, Vidal, Bayer, Feng, De La Cruz, Croci, Consalez, Mizumoto, and Hobert, in eLife (2017), analyze cholinergic ventral-nerve-cord motor-neuron classes in C. elegans and the roles of the terminal selector UNC-3 and Hox cofactors.
ocar.resolution: UNC-3 controls both shared class traits and subclass-specific genes along the anterior–posterior axis. Three of six worm Hox genes (lin-39, mab-5, egl-5) are expressed in subsets of DA, VA, and AS neurons and intersect with broadly expressed unc-3 to co-activate subclass effectors in post-mitotic motor neurons. The authors propose this intersectional logic may be conserved from nematodes to mice.
ocar.future_work: Conservation in mice is a stated possibility, not a result of this paper. How many subclass traits beyond the assayed genes follow the same logic remains open.

summaries.beginner: Motor neurons that look like one type still differ along a worm’s head-to-tail axis. This study shows a general identity gene working together with position genes to create those subtypes.
summaries.intermediate: Kratsios and colleagues (eLife, 2017) show that the COE-type terminal selector UNC-3 specifies both pan-class and subclass features of C. elegans cholinergic ventral-cord motor neurons. Region-restricted Hox proteins (lin-39, mab-5, egl-5) intersect with unc-3 in subsets of DA, VA, and AS neurons to co-activate subclass-specific effectors after mitosis. The discussion frames subclass diversification as more elusive than interclass specification and offers this intersectional strategy as a possible conserved principle.
summaries.advanced: Three of six C. elegans Hox genes are implicated in the assayed DA/VA/AS subclasses; that is not a complete motor-neuron atlas. Conservation to mice is hypothesized. Connectivity differences along the A-P axis are part of the subclass definition, but this paper is gene-regulatory, not a new EM connectome. White et al. 1986 is cited as the anatomical classification backdrop.

plain_language_summary: Motor neurons that look like one type still differ along a worm’s head-to-tail axis. This study shows a general identity gene working together with position genes to create those subtypes.

ocar.opportunity: Astrocytes are abundant regulators of synapse development and physiology, so a cell-biological account of how they contact and remodel synapses would clarify circuit construction.
ocar.challenge: Large gaps remain in astrocyte cell biology and in the mechanisms of astrocyte–synapse communication, leaving their role in brain function still poorly specified.
ocar.action: Allen and Eroglu, in Neuron (2017), review seminal findings on the cellular and molecular basis of astrocyte–neuron communication, focusing on synapse development and remodeling, and they list open questions.
ocar.resolution: They treat astrocytes as integral circuit components and essential regulators of synaptic development, summarizing morphological classes and known signaling interactions. The conclusion states that addressing the posed cell-biological questions is a step toward understanding how brains work.
ocar.future_work: The review explicitly defers mechanistic completeness to future work on the questions it raises; no new connectome or quantitative synapse census is provided.

summaries.beginner: Star-shaped brain cells called astrocytes help build and adjust synapses. This review gathers what is known about how they do that and lists what is still missing.
summaries.intermediate: Allen and Eroglu (Neuron, 2017) review the cell biology of astrocyte–synapse interactions in mammals, arguing that incomplete astrocyte cell biology limits understanding of brain function. They summarize evidence that astrocytes regulate synapse development and remodeling through bidirectional communication, note classical morphological categories of rodent astrocytes, and close by calling for work on the open mechanistic questions they pose. The PDF is an author manuscript.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not an original reconstruction. No numeric glia-to-synapse ratios are given in the extract. Catalog dimension is review. Adult neurogenic niches are mentioned as an exception where astrocytes participate in new-neuron integration, not as the paper’s experimental system.

plain_language_summary: Star-shaped brain cells called astrocytes help build and adjust synapses. This review gathers what is known about how they do that and lists what is still missing.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse anterior and midcingulate areas 24a/24b and 24a′/24b′ are implicated in cognition, emotion, and pain; a complete afferent–efferent map would give an anatomical basis for those functions.
ocar.challenge: Afferents of these areas had been described, but efferents needed a matching anterograde-tracing survey to finish the cingulate connectome and to compare ACC versus MCC and dorsal versus ventral subdivisions.
ocar.action: Fillinger, Yalcin, Barrot, and Veinante, in Brain Structure and Function (2017), as described in the catalog abstract, inject anterograde tracers into mouse areas 24a/24b (ACC) and 24a′/24b′ (MCC) and chart cortical and subcortical projections.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports a shared projection pattern to cortex, basal forebrain, hypothalamus, thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord, with denser ACC than MCC output and topographic differences between dorsal (24b/24b′) and ventral (24a/24a′) areas, suggesting shared plus area-specific roles.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the maps as the anatomical basis needed to address ACC/MCC function; causal tests are not claimed there.

summaries.beginner: This paper traces outgoing wires from mouse cingulate cortex and reports that neighboring cingulate patches share many targets but differ in how strongly and exactly they project.
summaries.intermediate: Fillinger, Yalcin, Barrot, and Veinante (Brain Structure and Function, 2017), as described in the catalog abstract, complete a mouse cingulate connectome by mapping efferents of ACC areas 24a/24b and MCC areas 24a′/24b′. Common targets include intracortical, basal-forebrain, hypothalamic, thalamic, brainstem, and spinal structures. ACC projections are overall denser than MCC, with further dorsal–ventral topography, supporting shared plus specialized functions.
summaries.advanced: PDF mismatch: the linked extract is Chintalacheruvu, Kalelkar, Alatriste-León, Boutin, Breton-Provencher, and Huda, Science Advances (2026), “The anterior cingulate cortex modulates pupil-linked arousal,” not Fillinger et al. 2017. This card uses the catalog abstract only. Target lists and density comparisons were not verified in a matching PDF.

plain_language_summary: This paper traces outgoing wires from mouse cingulate cortex and reports that neighboring cingulate patches share many targets but differ in how strongly and exactly they project.

ocar.opportunity: If monosynaptic excitatory connections onto interneurons can be inferred from spike timing in behaving animals, hippocampal E→I architecture and dynamics become accessible without full EM.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic connectivity is hard to study in vivo, and pairwise coupling estimates can be contaminated by background network co-modulation.
ocar.action: English, McKenzie, Evans, Kim, Yoon, and Buzsáki, in Neuron (2017), infer CA1 pyramidal-to-interneuron connectivity from spike transmission, and validate the inference with juxtacellular and optogenetic control of presynaptic spikes in behaving mice.
ocar.resolution: Neighboring CA1 cells had stronger connections; superficial pyramids projected more to deep interneurons. Connection probability and strength were skewed, with a minority of hubs. Divergence promoted interneuron synchrony; convergent synchrony boosted postsynaptic drive. Short-term depression and facilitation implemented diverse spike-transmission filters, and transmission depended on prior postsynaptic spike timing. Evoked spike-transmission probability tracked spontaneous coupling.
ocar.future_work: The discussion treats spike-timing inference as a complement to anatomical connectomics for dynamic synaptic parameters; a full anatomical census of the same pairs is not provided here.

summaries.beginner: This team infers which hippocampal cells talk to which inhibitory cells from the tiny delays between spikes, then checks the guesses by forcing single cells to fire in mice that are behaving.
summaries.intermediate: English and colleagues (Neuron, 2017) infer monosynaptic pyramidal-to-interneuron connections in mouse CA1 from spike timing and validate them with juxtacellular stimulation and optogenetics. They report stronger connections among neighbors, a superficial-pyramid to deep-interneuron bias, skewed hub-like connectivity, divergence-related interneuron synchrony, and diverse short-term synaptic filters. Discussion argues that spike-transmission probability for evoked spikes matches spontaneous coupling, supporting the timing-based method.
summaries.advanced: This is a physiological connectivity study, not an EM volume. Hub-like skew is qualitative in the abstract (no numeric degree distribution in the extract). Validation is for detectable spike transmission, which can miss weak synapses. The PDF is an author manuscript. μLED silicon probes (Kim/Yoon) are a recording technology, not the main scientific claim.

plain_language_summary: This team infers which hippocampal cells talk to which inhibitory cells from the tiny delays between spikes, then checks the guesses by forcing single cells to fire in mice that are behaving.

ocar.opportunity: Cleared thick sections could be imaged fast enough to map whole mouse brains at synaptic-spine resolution, including with immunofluorescence for cell-type-specific maps.
ocar.challenge: Conventional sectioning plus confocal is slow at brain scale; light-sheet methods must keep resolution while scanning large, moving samples.
ocar.action: Wang, Zhu, Ding, Shen, Yang, Xu, Shu, Guo, Xiong, Shan, Jia, Su, Yang, Li, Cheng, He, Chen, Wu, Zhou, Xu, Han, Lau, and Bi, in National Science Review (2019; catalog lists bioRxiv 2017), describe synchronized scanning illumination and oblique imaging of cleared thick tissue in continuous motion.
ocar.resolution: They report high-speed 3D acquisition of an entire mouse brain within 2 hours at a resolution capable of resolving synaptic spines, compatibility with immunofluorescence, and scalability toward samples such as primate brain. Using the system they examined c-Fos-shEGFP activation in 16 mice at rest or after forced swimming, finding multi-area subcortical involvement in stress with striking individual variability.
ocar.future_work: Individual variability is used to argue for sufficient cohort size; primate-brain scaling is stated as compatibility, not a completed primate dataset. The extract’s tail is references.

summaries.beginner: This microscope scans a whole cleared mouse brain in about two hours, sharp enough to see dendritic spines, and is used to compare which cells turned on after a stressful swim.
summaries.intermediate: Wang and colleagues (National Science Review, 2019) present a light-sheet method with synchronized scanning illumination and oblique imaging of cleared thick sections in smooth motion. They report whole-mouse-brain acquisition within 2 hours at synaptic-spine resolution and immunofluorescence compatibility. In 16 c-Fos-shEGFP mice, resting versus forced-swimming conditions implicated multiple subcortical areas in stress responses, with large individual variability. Catalog metadata list bioRxiv 2017; the PDF is the NSR research article (doi 10.1093/nsr/nwz053).
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s discussion is not captured (tail is references). “Within 2 hours” and spine resolution are abstract claims; voxel size is not in the extract. n = 16 is the c-Fos cohort, not a connectomic reconstruction. Primate-brain scalability is prospective. Catalog dimension is image-acquisition.

plain_language_summary: This microscope scans a whole cleared mouse brain in about two hours, sharp enough to see dendritic spines, and is used to compare which cells turned on after a stressful swim.

ocar.opportunity: Divergent feedforward networks that separate overlapping activity patterns are common, and they share similarly sparse synaptic connectivity, as in cerebellar granule layer.
ocar.challenge: Marr–Albus theory emphasizes expansion and sparse activity, but spatial correlations in input and connectivity may undermine separation; the relative contribution of sparse synapses versus sparse firing was unclear.
ocar.action: Cayco-Gajic, Clopath, and Silver, in Nature Communications (2017), build cerebellar input-layer models with spatially correlated inputs, systematically vary synaptic connectivity, and score pattern separation by how fast a classifier learns input versus output patterns.
ocar.resolution: Sparse synaptic connectivity was essential for separating spatially correlated inputs over a wide activity range. Expansion and correlations, rather than sparse activity, were the major determinants of pattern separation.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s tail is references; generality beyond cerebellar input-layer architecture should be checked in the full discussion rather than assumed.

summaries.beginner: Brain networks that pull similar patterns apart often use very few synapses per cell. Models of the cerebellum’s input layer here show that those sparse wires, not just quiet firing, are what make the patterns separable.
summaries.intermediate: Cayco-Gajic, Clopath, and Silver (Nature Communications, 2017) model the cerebellar input layer with spatially correlated inputs and vary synaptic connectivity. Pattern-separation performance is the learning speed of a classifier on input versus output patterns. Sparse connectivity is required across a wide activity range; expansion recoding and correlation structure outweigh sparse activity as the main drivers, contrary to a purely Marr–Albus sparse-coding emphasis.
summaries.advanced: Results are from reduced and detailed spiking models, not a new EM connectome. The extract’s discussion is missing (references only). “Major determinants” is the authors’ ranking from their parameter sweeps; numeric classifier scores are not in the selected text. Cerebellar anatomy is the explicit case; other divergent networks are motivational.

plain_language_summary: Brain networks that pull similar patterns apart often use very few synapses per cell. Models of the cerebellum’s input layer here show that those sparse wires, not just quiet firing, are what make the patterns separable.

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks can segment biomedical images well, but each new modality or organ usually needs a new expert-labeled training set.
ocar.challenge: Annotation time is scarce; the question is which pixels to label next to reach the best accuracy under a budget.
ocar.action: Yang, Zhang, Chen, Zhang, and Chen, at MICCAI (2017), combine fully convolutional networks with active learning, using FCN uncertainty and similarity to pose a generalized maximum set-cover problem that selects representative, uncertain regions.
ocar.resolution: On the 2015 MICCAI Gland Challenge and a lymph-node ultrasound dataset, their annotation suggestions reached then-current state-of-the-art segmentation using only 50% of the training data. Simulated budgets of 10%, 30%, and 50% of labeled pixels beat random query and uncertainty-only query. Full-data FCN improved about 2% on four gland metrics and was about 0.5% worse on two.
ocar.future_work: The framework is demonstrated on 2D gland and ultrasound images; extension to large 3D EM connectomics volumes is not shown here.

summaries.beginner: Labeling biomedical images for a computer is slow and needs experts. This method asks which regions to label next so that half as much drawing still matches a fully labeled training set.
summaries.intermediate: Yang and colleagues (MICCAI 2017; arXiv:1706.04737v1) present suggestive annotation: FCNs plus active learning that selects uncertain and representative areas via a generalized maximum set-cover formulation. On MICCAI gland data and lymph-node ultrasound, suggested labels reached SOTA with 50% of training data. Simulated 10/30/50% pixel budgets outperformed random and uncertainty-only querying. Experiment settings in the extract include k = 8, K = 16, four FCNs, and a 5% validation split.
summaries.advanced: “State-of-the-art” is relative to the 2017 gland-challenge numbers plotted as a dashed line, not a later transformer baseline. Gains of ~2% / ~0.5% are for the full-data FCN module versus then-current full-data methods, not for the 50% budget. Waiting time between suggestion stages is given as 10 minutes on four Tesla P100 GPUs. This is not a neuronal EM segmentation paper despite the catalog segmentation tag.

plain_language_summary: Labeling biomedical images for a computer is slow and needs experts. This method asks which regions to label next so that half as much drawing still matches a fully labeled training set.

ocar.opportunity: Optogenetic engram studies emphasize which neurons fire and join ensembles, not only which synapses potentiate, suggesting a broader cellular view of learning.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic plasticity (e.g., LTP) is often treated as the cellular correlate of learning, which can underweight cell-autonomous excitability changes.
ocar.action: Titley, Brunel, and Hansel, in Neuron (2017), review evidence that ensemble integration can arise from LTP or from intrinsic membrane-excitability plasticity, and they propose distinct roles for the two.
ocar.resolution: They argue that synaptic plasticity sets connectivity maps while intrinsic plasticity, possibly separated in time, amplifies responsiveness and acutely drives engram integration—a move from an exclusively synaptocentric toward a non-exclusive neurocentric view. They note a lower induction threshold for some intrinsic plasticity (Purkinje-cell examples inducible within 3 s) and that excitability changes can contribute to a memory trace with little ongoing synaptic involvement after induction.
ocar.future_work: Whether intrinsic plasticity commonly supports single-experience learning in adult associative systems remains a proposed scenario. Adult synaptic rewiring is described as typically slower, over days.

summaries.beginner: Learning is often explained as stronger synapses. This review argues that neurons can also join a memory by becoming easier to fire, even without rewriting their connections first.
summaries.intermediate: Titley, Brunel, and Hansel (Neuron, 2017) review engram-cell studies and intrinsic plasticity. They propose that synaptic plasticity determines connectivity maps while intrinsic plasticity amplifies responses and can acutely integrate neurons into ensembles, possibly on a faster timescale than synaptic rewiring. The extract cites Purkinje-cell intrinsic plasticity inducible within 3 s as evidence of a lower threshold than typical synaptic plasticity. The PDF is an author manuscript.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective/review, not a new physiology dataset. The 3 s Purkinje-cell figure is cited from prior work (Belmeguenai et al., 2010; Ohtsuki et al., 2012; Lopez-Rojas et al., 2016), not measured here. “Neurocentric” is the authors’ framing. Catalog dimension is review.

plain_language_summary: Learning is often explained as stronger synapses. This review argues that neurons can also join a memory by becoming easier to fire, even without rewriting their connections first.

ocar.opportunity: Basal forebrain (BF) neurons contribute to sleep–wake, attention, and learning, but cell-type-specific long-range wiring that could explain those functions was incomplete.
ocar.challenge: Cholinergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic (PV+ and SOM+) neurons are intermingled, so mixed tracing cannot assign inputs and outputs to types.
ocar.action: Do, Xu, Lee, Chang, Zhang, Chung, Yung, Fan, Miyamichi, Luo, and Dan, in eLife (2016), map inputs with rabies monosynaptic retrograde tracing and outputs with AAV axonal tracing for four BF cell types in mouse, with data at sleepcircuits.org/bf/.
ocar.resolution: Inputs to the four types were qualitatively similar (cortical input mainly from agranular insular and orbital prefrontal cortex), whereas outputs differed markedly. Connections of glutamatergic and SOM+ neurons were strongly reciprocal; those of cholinergic and PV+ neurons were more unidirectional. Rabies tracing showed extensive monosynaptic prefrontal innervation of cholinergic neurons, contrary to a prior ultrastructural negative report, and was backed by electrophysiology.
ocar.future_work: The maps supply candidate sources of reinforcement signals to BF cholinergic neurons; which of those sources actually carry task reward is not identified here.

summaries.beginner: The basal forebrain has several cell types mixed together. This mouse study maps who talks to each type and finds similar incoming wires but very different outgoing wires.
summaries.intermediate: Do and colleagues (eLife, 2016) perform whole-brain input and output mapping of mouse BF cholinergic, glutamatergic, PV+, and SOM+ neurons (rabies plus AAV). Inputs are qualitatively similar across types; outputs diverge. Glutamatergic and SOM+ connections are strongly reciprocal, cholinergic and PV+ more one-way. Discussion highlights prefrontal agranular insular/orbital sources to all four types and rabies-plus-physiology evidence for monosynaptic prefrontal contacts onto cholinergic cells, against an earlier ultrastructural miss. Resource: sleepcircuits.org/bf/.
summaries.advanced: “Qualitatively similar” inputs still allow quantitative differences not listed in the extract. Reciprocal versus unidirectional is a summary of the projection graphs, not a synaptic EM proof of reciprocity at terminals. The website URL is as printed in 2016 and may have moved. Catalog dimension is cell-types.

plain_language_summary: The basal forebrain has several cell types mixed together. This mouse study maps who talks to each type and finds similar incoming wires but very different outgoing wires.

ocar.opportunity: Neural connectomes share modular organization and rich-club hubs; those anatomical ingredients might explain complex collective dynamics.
ocar.challenge: Destroying either modules or hubs in surrogates is needed to test whether both are required for functional complexity, and empirical rest should be compared with the maximum complexity the anatomy can host.
ocar.action: Zamora-López, Chen, Deco, Kringelbach, and Zhou, in Scientific Reports (2016), compare C. elegans, cat, macaque, and human connectomes to module- or hub-destroyed surrogates, compare simulated versus empirical human resting-state FC, and introduce a hierarchical model that routes cross-modular links by preferential attachment.
ocar.resolution: Functional complexity always decreased when modules or hubs were destroyed. Human rest is described as occupying a dynamical state reflecting the largest complexity its anatomical connectome can host. The hierarchical model hosted more complex dynamics than other widely used hierarchical benchmarks. Their complexity measure is proposed as a clinical marker because it needs no arbitrary binarization threshold.
ocar.future_work: Clinical-marker use is prospective. C. elegans analysis used a cleaned Varshney collation (N = 275 neurons, L = 2990 links after dropping neurons with no inputs; density ρ = 0.04).

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring is grouped into modules and a club of busy hubs. This study shows that both ingredients help the network produce rich activity patterns, and it offers a simple score of that richness.
summaries.intermediate: Zamora-López and colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2016) ask how modules and rich-club hubs shape dynamics on C. elegans, cat, macaque, and human connectomes. Surrogates that destroy either ingredient reduce functional complexity. Simulated versus empirical human resting-state FC is taken to show rest near the anatomy’s maximum hosted complexity. A hierarchical model with preferential-attachment cross-modular links outperforms other hierarchical benchmarks. Outlook proposes the complexity measure as a threshold-free clinical marker.
summaries.advanced: C. elegans numbers in the extract (N = 275, L = 2990, ρ = 0.04, 47% reciprocal among remaining links as stated) are after the authors’ cleaning of Varshney et al., not the raw 302-neuron census. “Largest complexity its anatomical connectome can host” is a comparison within their simulations, not a unique brain optimum. Clinical translation is not demonstrated. The extract’s outlook is interleaved with a methods description of the worm network.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring is grouped into modules and a club of busy hubs. This study shows that both ingredients help the network produce rich activity patterns, and it offers a simple score of that richness.

ocar.opportunity: Among C. elegans sex-shared neurons, PHC shows the largest sexually dimorphic connectivity, becoming a densely connected hub sensory/interneuron in males.
ocar.challenge: Whether that hub identity is cell-autonomous and which conserved transcription factor executes the male program was unknown.
ocar.action: Serrano-Saiz, Oren-Suissa, Bayer, and Hobert, on bioRxiv (2016, doi 10.1101/081083), describe male-specific scaling of synaptic-vesicle machinery (including eat-4/VGLUT), neuropeptide induction, axon-morphology change, and a functional switch in PHC, and they test the Doublesex homolog dmd-3.
ocar.resolution: dmd-3 is required and sufficient for male-specific PHC differentiation, including synaptic-machinery scaling. Cellular specificity comes from collaboration with non-sex-specific terminal selectors; sex specificity comes from TRA-1 repression of dmd-3 in hermaphrodite PHC. The remodeling is cell-autonomous and independent of other network components.
ocar.future_work: dmd-3 also acts in skin and other male-specific cells, so context dependence of the same factor remains a comparative question. Scaling of panneuronal synaptic genes had been considered robust; this exception invites broader tests.

summaries.beginner: A sensory neuron present in both worm sexes becomes a busy hub only in males. One conserved sex-determining gene, acting inside that cell, is enough to flip on the male wiring program.
summaries.intermediate: Serrano-Saiz, Oren-Suissa, Bayer, and Hobert (bioRxiv 2016) show that C. elegans PHC differentiates into a male hub by scaling synaptic-vesicle components (including eat-4/VGLUT), inducing neuropeptides, remodeling axons, and switching function. The Doublesex homolog dmd-3 is necessary and sufficient cell-autonomously; TRA-1 represses dmd-3 in hermaphrodites, and non-sex-specific terminal selectors supply cellular context. Discussion emphasizes that PHC’s dimorphism exceeds other sex-shared sensory neurons such as PHA/PHB.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint (posted 14 October 2016), not the later journal version if one exists. “Largest extent of sexually dimorphic connectivity” cites prior connectome work ([6] in the preprint), not a new EM volume. Sufficiency of dmd-3 is for the assayed PHC program. Catalog dimension is graph-analysis; the paper is developmental genetics.

plain_language_summary: A sensory neuron present in both worm sexes becomes a busy hub only in males. One conserved sex-determining gene, acting inside that cell, is enough to flip on the male wiring program.

ocar.opportunity: Super-resolution fluorescence deep in tissue would let synaptic circuits be mapped optically if scattering and spherical aberration can be controlled.
ocar.challenge: Standard mounting mismatches the refractive index of immersion oil (1.518), limiting super-resolution depth.
ocar.action: Ke, Nakai, Fujimoto, Takayama, Yoshida, Kitajima, Sato, and Imai, in Cell Reports (2016), as described in the catalog abstract, introduce SeeDB2, an index-optimized clearing agent matched to oil immersion, and apply volumetric super-resolution imaging to mouse neurons and fly medulla.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports preservation of fine morphology and fluorescent proteins, super-resolution to depths >100 μm (an order of magnitude deeper than standard mounting), accumulation of inhibitory synapses on spine heads in NMDA-receptor-deficient neurons, and unexpected heterogeneity of Mi1 axon-bouton orientations in the fly motion circuit.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents volumetric super-resolution of cleared tissue as a strategy for synaptic-level connectomics; EM-level completeness is not claimed there.

summaries.beginner: Seeing synapses with a light microscope deep inside tissue is usually blurry. This paper introduces a clearing recipe that matches oil-immersion lenses so super-resolution can go more than ten times deeper.
summaries.intermediate: Ke and colleagues (Cell Reports, 2016), as described in the catalog abstract, develop SeeDB2 to match fixed-tissue refractive index to immersion oil (1.518). They report super-resolution imaging >100 μm deep with preserved morphology and fluorescent proteins, extra inhibitory synapses on spine heads in NMDA-receptor-deficient neurons, and heterogeneous Mi1 bouton orientations in Drosophila medulla. The work is positioned as optical connectomics at synaptic scale.
summaries.advanced: PDF mismatch: the linked extract is Aizawa, Shimamoto, Kajikawa, Hara, Abe, Shibuya, and Kitajima on dynamic blebbing during mouse oocyte formation, not Ke et al. 2016 SeeDB2. This card uses the catalog abstract only. Depth (>100 μm) and biological findings were not verified in a matching PDF.

plain_language_summary: Seeing synapses with a light microscope deep inside tissue is usually blurry. This paper introduces a clearing recipe that matches oil-immersion lenses so super-resolution can go more than ten times deeper.

ocar.opportunity: Large graphs in neuroscience and social networks are thought to be built from loosely coupled subgraphs whose repeated motifs can be detected and classified.
ocar.challenge: Community detection alone does not say which communities are structurally the same; a hierarchical model and a comparison method are needed.
ocar.action: Lyzinski, Tang, Athreya, Park, and Priebe, in IEEE Transactions on Network Science and Engineering (2016; arXiv 2015/2016), embed a graph, cluster vertices, compare communities with nonparametric graph inference, and recurse, analyzing a hierarchical stochastic blockmodel with consistency conditions, then apply the method to a partially reconstructed Drosophila connectome and to Friendster.
ocar.resolution: They establish conditions for consistent parameter and motif estimates in the hierarchical SBM and report that the algorithm locates similar sub-communities in the fly connectome and in Friendster.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s tail is a proof sketch, so empirical cluster counts and error rates should be taken from the full paper’s experiments. The cortical-column conjecture is cited as motivation, not as a dataset they fully test.

summaries.beginner: This statistics paper finds groups inside a network, then asks which groups are built the same way, repeating the process to reveal a hierarchy—illustrated on a fly brain graph and a social network.
summaries.intermediate: Lyzinski and colleagues (IEEE TNSE, 2016) propose recursive embedding, clustering, and nonparametric graph comparison to detect and classify communities in a hierarchical stochastic blockmodel, with theoretical consistency conditions. They apply the procedure to a partially reconstructed Drosophila connectome and to Friendster to find similar sub-communities. Neuroscience is an explicit motivation (vertices as neurons or regions; cortical-column conjecture).
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s second half is mathematical proof, not the Drosophila results section, so fly and Friendster findings follow the abstract. “Partially reconstructed Drosophila connectome” is not sized here. Catalog dimension is image-acquisition, which does not match the paper’s graph-inference content. arXiv version in the extract is 1503.02115v5 (26 Aug 2016).

plain_language_summary: This statistics paper finds groups inside a network, then asks which groups are built the same way, repeating the process to reveal a hierarchy—illustrated on a fly brain graph and a social network.

ocar.opportunity: Focal epilepsies increasingly look like network diseases, so individual connectomes assessed with graph theory could become diagnostic and treatment biomarkers.
ocar.challenge: Translational measurement of abnormal networks had been limited by methods; connectomics now offers person-specific maps but produces complex “big data.”
ocar.action: Gleichgerrcht, Kocher, and Bonilha, in Epilepsia (2015), as described in the catalog abstract, review emerging connectomics evidence on architecture, dynamics, and function in epilepsy and discuss links to conceptual models and personalized care.
ocar.resolution: The abstract argues that graph analysis of the personal connectome can reveal organization prone to abnormal dynamics and epileptogenesis, that a rapidly growing evidence base already addresses fundamental aspects of epileptic networks, and that unique per-subject network information may help explain outcome variability.
ocar.future_work: The abstract stresses the need for collaborative, rigorous evaluation of connectomic big data to realize personalized medicine; no single new cohort is reported there.

summaries.beginner: Epilepsy often involves whole-brain networks, not just one damaged spot. This review explains how mapping a person’s brain connections with network math might eventually guide diagnosis and treatment.
summaries.intermediate: Gleichgerrcht, Kocher, and Bonilha (Epilepsia, 2015), as described in the catalog abstract, review MRI/connectomic and graph-theoretic studies of epilepsy. They argue that network endophenotypes could be biomarkers, that connectomics can test hypotheses from basic models of epileptogenesis, and that individual connectomes may inform variable surgical or medical outcomes. They call for collaborative analysis of rich per-subject data.
summaries.advanced: PDF mismatch: the linked extract is Wang, Li, Li, Yu, Jiang, Zhou, Hu, Yang, Chen, Yang, and Wang, Epilepsia (DOI 10.1002/epi.70065), a 1919-child MRI-negative pediatric epilepsy morphometry study, not Gleichgerrcht et al. 2015. This card uses the catalog abstract only. No graph-theory metrics from the 2015 review were verified in a matching PDF.

plain_language_summary: Epilepsy often involves whole-brain networks, not just one damaged spot. This review explains how mapping a person’s brain connections with network math might eventually guide diagnosis and treatment.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical population activity occupies a lower-dimensional space than the combinatorial explosion of spike patterns; a simple per-neuron coupling statistic could summarize that structure.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether neighboring neurons share the same relationship to the population, and whether that relationship reflects stimulus preference, behavior, causality, and synapses.
ocar.action: Okun, Steinmetz, Cossell, Iacaruso, Ko, Barthó, Moore, Hofer, Mrsic-Flogel, Carandini, and Harris, in Nature (2015), record visual cortex in mouse and monkey and relate each cell’s population coupling to behavior, optogenetic drive, in vitro synaptic counts, and pairwise correlations.
ocar.resolution: Neighbors ranged from strongly coupled “choristers” to weakly coupled “soloists.” Coupling was largely independent of sensory preference and invariant to stimulus conditions. Highly coupled cells were more affected by non-sensory variables such as motor intention. Coupling predicted responses to optogenetic increases in local activity and predicted in vitro neighbor-synapse counts. Knowledge of n neurons’ couplings predicted a substantial portion of their n² pairwise correlations; residual correlations still tracked orientation similarity after removing nonspecific connectivity predictions.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s tail is figure/supplementary-style correlation analyses; a full circuit model of how coupling is wired is not a new EM reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: Even neighboring visual-cortex cells differ: some fire with the crowd (“choristers”) and some do not (“soloists”). That simple difference predicts extra synapses, sensitivity to movement, and much of the pairwise correlation structure.
summaries.intermediate: Okun and colleagues (Nature, 2015) define population coupling in mouse and monkey visual cortex. Coupling is a stable cellular attribute, largely independent of sensory tuning, higher in cells more affected by motor intention, causally predictive of optogenetic population drive, and predictive of in vitro synapses from neighbors. Coupling of n cells predicts much of the n² correlation matrix; leftover correlations still depend on orientation difference, matching a specific-plus-nonspecific connectivity picture. The PDF is a Europe PMC author manuscript.
summaries.advanced: “Substantial portion” of pairwise correlations is not given as a single R² in the extract. In vitro synapse counts are subsequent estimates on the same neurons, not a complete connectome. Species are Mus musculus and Macaca mulatta. Catalog dimension is connectomics; the measurements are physiological plus slice connectivity, not volume EM.

plain_language_summary: Even neighboring visual-cortex cells differ: some fire with the crowd (“choristers”) and some do not (“soloists”). That simple difference predicts extra synapses, sensitivity to movement, and much of the pairwise correlation structure.

ocar.opportunity: Graph matching, a quadratic assignment problem, is needed to align large brain-graphs such as C. elegans connectomes as graph-valued data grow.
ocar.challenge: QAPs are NP-hard; prior approximations were too slow or too inaccurate for big-data graphs.
ocar.action: Vogelstein, Conroy, Lyzinski, Podrazik, Kratzer, Harley, Fishkind, R. J. Vogelstein, and Priebe, in PLoS ONE (2015), introduce the Fast Approximate Quadratic assignment (FAQ) algorithm and benchmark it on QAPLIB and on matching C. elegans connectomes.
ocar.resolution: FAQ was faster and achieved a lower objective value on over 80% of the QAPLIB library versus the previous state of the art, and it efficiently achieved performance on the worm connectome matching task. The discussion lists extensions: parallel LAP subroutines, sparsity, vertex attributes (position, cell type), and matching more than two graphs.
ocar.future_work: Multiple-graph matching is described as in progress. Incorporating biological vertex attributes is proposed, not demonstrated as a completed brain-atlas pipeline.

summaries.beginner: Lining up two wiring diagrams is a hard matching problem. This algorithm does it faster and, on a standard test set, better than the previous champion, including on worm brain graphs.
summaries.intermediate: Vogelstein and colleagues (PLoS ONE, 2015) present FAQ for approximate quadratic assignment / graph matching. Empirically it is faster and attains a lower objective on over 80% of QAPLIB instances than the prior state of the art, and it is applied to matching C. elegans connectomes (data linked in the paper). Concluding remarks emphasize Frank–Wolfe-style optimization, LAP subproblems, and planned use of vertex attributes such as brain position and cell type.
summaries.advanced: “Over 80% of QAPLIB” is an aggregate win rate, not a guarantee on every instance. Worm matching “efficiently achieves performance” is not given as a numeric accuracy in the abstract extract. Catalog dimension is graph-analysis. C. elegans data URL is the authors’ GitHub path as printed in 2015.

plain_language_summary: Lining up two wiring diagrams is a hard matching problem. This algorithm does it faster and, on a standard test set, better than the previous champion, including on worm brain graphs.

ocar.opportunity: Excitatory afferents onto cerebellar Purkinje cells occupy stereotyped, non-overlapping synaptic territories; a secreted ligand–receptor pair could explain that patterning.
ocar.challenge: What sets synapse number, morphology, and subcellular localization for parallel-fiber versus climbing-fiber inputs was unclear.
ocar.action: Sigoillot, Iyer, Binda, González-Calvo, Talleur, Vodjdani, Isope, and Selimi, in Cell Reports (2015), as described in the catalog abstract, study the complement C1Q-related protein C1QL1 and its receptor BAI3 in mouse cerebellum.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that BAI3 modulates synaptogenesis of both parallel-fiber and climbing-fiber afferents, while timely, restricted C1QL1 expression in inferior olivary neurons assigns climbing-fiber territory. Given broad C1QL/BAI expression, they propose a general mechanism for building functional connectivity.
ocar.future_work: Generality beyond cerebellum is inferred from expression, not demonstrated in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Two kinds of excitatory input land on cerebellar Purkinje cells in tidy, separate zones. This paper identifies a secreted protein and its receptor that help set those territories.
summaries.intermediate: Sigoillot and colleagues (Cell Reports, 2015), as described in the catalog abstract, show that C1QL1 and its adhesion-GPCR receptor BAI3 control excitatory connectivity onto Purkinje cells. BAI3 affects both parallel-fiber and climbing-fiber synaptogenesis; olivary C1QL1 expression timing and restriction position climbing fibers. Broad C1QL/BAI expression is taken to suggest a general wiring mechanism.
summaries.advanced: PDF mismatch: the linked extract is Baum, Bodnya, Costanzo, and Gama, bioRxiv (2024.08.23.609462), on patient DRP1 mutations and cortical synaptic maturation, not Sigoillot et al. 2015. This card uses the catalog abstract only. Synapse counts and olivary expression timing were not verified in a matching PDF.

plain_language_summary: Two kinds of excitatory input land on cerebellar Purkinje cells in tidy, separate zones. This paper identifies a secreted protein and its receptor that help set those territories.

ocar.opportunity: Synchronization on the empirical human connectome could explain flexible access to many dynamical repertoires without fine-tuning to a critical point.
ocar.challenge: Standard Kuramoto dynamics on simpler networks miss the hierarchical modular structure and frequency heterogeneity of the connectome.
ocar.action: Villegas, Moretti, and Muñoz, in Scientific Reports (2014), study Kuramoto synchronization analytically and computationally on the human connectome and on synthetic hierarchical modular networks, using spectral graph theory to interpret slow modes.
ocar.resolution: They report an intermediate phase between order and disorder, arising from hierarchical modules plus quenched frequency heterogeneity: frustrated synchronization, metastability, and chimera-like states. Structural bottlenecks at many scales produce anomalously slow dynamics; even the coarse-grained connectome shows non-degenerate Laplacian eigenvalues at the lower edge as a fingerprint of that heterogeneity. Without frequency dispersion, synthetic hierarchies synchronize bottom-up; bottlenecks alter that cascade.
ocar.future_work: Relating these mesoscopic chimera-like regimes to cognitive flexibility is interpretive. The connectome used is a coarse-grained mapping, not cellular resolution.

summaries.beginner: When simple oscillator models run on a map of human white-matter connections, they do not just lock together or fall apart. A messy in-between regime appears, with parts of the network aligning while others drift.
summaries.intermediate: Villegas, Moretti, and Muñoz (Scientific Reports, 2014) simulate and analyze Kuramoto dynamics on the human connectome and on hierarchical modular surrogates. Hierarchical organization plus frequency heterogeneity yields frustrated synchronization, metastability, and chimera-like states between the usual coherent and incoherent phases. Spectral graph theory links the slow dynamics to structural bottlenecks and to non-degenerate small Laplacian eigenvalues. The discussion treats this complexity as a way for the brain to access many attractors without sitting exactly at criticality.
summaries.advanced: This is a mesoscopic oscillator model on a region-level connectome, not neural spikes or EM. “Chimera-like” is the authors’ analogy. No subject count or parcellation size appears in the selected extract. arXiv version in the file is 1402.5289v2 (3 Jul 2014). Catalog year is 2014.

plain_language_summary: When simple oscillator models run on a map of human white-matter connections, they do not just lock together or fall apart. A messy in-between regime appears, with parts of the network aligning while others drift.

ocar.opportunity: Golgi-Cox staining visualizes dendritic spines across species, including humans, with simple optics, so an objective classifier would make developmental and disease studies more comparable.
ocar.challenge: Manual spine typing is slow and inconsistent because categories are loosely defined.
ocar.action: Risher, Ustunkaya, Singh Alvarado, and Eroglu, in PLoS ONE (2014), define a geometry-based hierarchical formula on measurements exported from RECONSTRUCT and test it on mouse primary visual cortex during development.
ocar.resolution: The formula conveyed the maturational shift in spine types. Versus a trained observer on the same dendrites, filopodia density did not differ (0.07±0.01 versus 0.06±0.01 per unit length; p = 0.50) nor did mushroom density (0.25±0.02 versus 0.28±0.02; p = 0.37). Spreadsheets implement length-to-width ratio and type rules. Remaining drawbacks include stain time up to 2.5 weeks.
ocar.future_work: The method still depends on Golgi-Cox’s incomplete labeling and on 2D measurements from light micrographs, not EM-verified spine classes.

summaries.beginner: Sorting dendritic spines into shapes by eye is slow and disagreeable. This paper uses simple length and width rules in a spreadsheet so the typing is faster and less subjective.
summaries.intermediate: Risher, Ustunkaya, Singh Alvarado, and Eroglu (PLoS ONE, 2014) introduce a rapid Golgi spine-classification method using objective geometry and freely available tools (RECONSTRUCT plus spreadsheet formulas). In mouse V1 it captured developmental maturation of spine types. Formula-versus-expert densities matched for filopodia (p = 0.50) and mushrooms (p = 0.37) on the same dendrites. They discuss remaining Golgi-Cox time cost (staining up to 2.5 weeks) and analyst-to-analyst inconsistency of purely visual typing.
summaries.advanced: Densities in the extract are printed as 0.07±0.01 and 0.06±0.01 (filopodia) and 0.25±0.02 and 0.28±0.02 (mushrooms); the unit is given as per mm in the OCR and likely denotes per µm of dendrite—treat the unit with caution. Comparison is to one trained observer (W.C.R.). This is light-microscopy morphology, not synaptic EM. Catalog dimension is image-acquisition.

plain_language_summary: Sorting dendritic spines into shapes by eye is slow and disagreeable. This paper uses simple length and width rules in a spreadsheet so the typing is faster and less subjective.

ocar.opportunity: Human connectome research has been paced by visualization innovations, from diffusion glyphs to tract renderings to graph views of functional connectivity.
ocar.challenge: Unresolved tensions remain: probabilistic versus deterministic tractography’s visual appeal, multimodal reduction, clutter when rendering a full connectome in anatomical space, and trade-offs among anatomy versus topology, aesthetics versus information, and thoroughness versus readability.
ocar.action: Margulies, Böttger, Watanabe, and Gorgolewski, in NeuroImage (2013), as described in the catalog abstract, review visualization methods for anatomical and functional connectivity, survey interactive research tools, and discuss concerns in presenting connectivity results.
ocar.resolution: The abstract frames visualization as enabling intuitive insight while documenting persistent problems and the need to negotiate those design tensions.
ocar.future_work: The abstract points to ongoing development of interactive tools and to unresolved presentation issues rather than a single software release.

summaries.beginner: Maps of human brain connections are only as useful as the pictures that show them. This review walks through how those pictures evolved and why they still get cluttered or misleading.
summaries.intermediate: Margulies, Böttger, Watanabe, and Gorgolewski (NeuroImage, 2013), as described in the catalog abstract, survey visualization of the human connectome: tensor glyphs, anatomical tract rendering, and graph-based functional connectivity. They discuss unresolved problems (probabilistic tractography’s weaker visual appeal, multimodal reduction, anatomical clutter) and tensions between anatomic versus connectomic emphasis, aesthetics versus information, and completeness versus readability, plus available interactive tools.
summaries.advanced: PDF mismatch: the linked extract is de Ridder, Klein, and Kim, Brain Informatics (2018), a review of visual analytics for uncertainties in fMRI, not Margulies et al. 2013. This card uses the catalog abstract only. Named visualization tools from the NeuroImage paper were not verified in a matching PDF.

plain_language_summary: Maps of human brain connections are only as useful as the pictures that show them. This review walks through how those pictures evolved and why they still get cluttered or misleading.

ocar.opportunity: Neocortical layer 6B is heterogeneous and understudied; a quantitative morphological–physiological classification would enable later connectivity work.
ocar.challenge: Prior names for the layer are not interchangeable, and few studies used unsupervised classification focused on excitatory L6B cells.
ocar.action: Marx and Feldmeyer, in Cerebral Cortex (advance access 2012; issue date December 2013), combine whole-cell recording and biocytin filling in P17–24 rat somatosensory barrel cortex, then unsupervised cluster analysis on physiology plus axonal and dendritic metrics.
ocar.resolution: Three excitatory clusters emerged: (C1) pyramids with pia-directed apical dendrites; (C2) cells with a prominent “apical-like” dendrite not aimed at the pia (further split into inverted, tangentially oriented, and horizontally oriented); (C3) multipolar spiny neurons. L6B pyramids further split by axonal domain into more column-confined versus extended. The authors compare L6B types to developmental subplate classes.
ocar.future_work: The classification is offered as a basis for future structure–function and synaptic-connectivity studies; those connectivity maps are not in this paper.

summaries.beginner: A deep, overlooked cortical layer contains mixed excitatory cell shapes. This rat study sorts them into three main groups using both their anatomy and their electrical properties.
summaries.intermediate: Marx and Feldmeyer (Cerebral Cortex, 2013) classify excitatory layer 6B neurons in adolescent rat barrel cortex with patch recording, biocytin reconstructions, and unsupervised clustering. They report pia-directed pyramids, neurons with misoriented apical-like dendrites (inverted, tangential, horizontal), and multipolar spiny cells, plus two axonal-field subtypes of pyramids. Discussion argues P17–24 morphology is nearly adult and compares L6B types to subplate neurons.
summaries.advanced: Sample size of reconstructed cells is not in the selected extract. Clustering features mix physiology and morphology; alternative feature sets could shift boundaries. Slice recordings omit long axons cut by sectioning. Catalog year is 2012 (advance access); the PDF header is the December 2013 issue (23:2803–2817).

plain_language_summary: A deep, overlooked cortical layer contains mixed excitatory cell shapes. This rat study sorts them into three main groups using both their anatomy and their electrical properties.

ocar.opportunity: Knowing how far excitatory and inhibitory connections spread in mouse A1 would show whether local circuits favor lateral inhibition or co-tuned excitation and inhibition.
ocar.challenge: In vivo reports disagree, most dual recordings sampled only neighbors closer than about 100 μm, and slicing truncates processes.
ocar.action: Levy and Reyes, in Journal of Neuroscience (2012), use multiple intracellular recording in mouse primary auditory cortical slices to map connectivity among pyramids, fast-spiking (FS), and non-FS cells in the principal input layer, fit distance dependence with Gaussians, and estimate truncation effects from anatomy.
ocar.resolution: Connection probability was distance-dependent with comparable Gaussian spreads of 85–114 μm across cell types. FS-formed unitary synapses were stronger than other classes during brief trains; strength did not correlate with distance. Anatomy qualitatively matched physiology. Slicing reduced overall connectivity but did not change the spatial pattern. Comparable E and I spreads plus strong E–I interconnectivity are consistent with models in which either lateral inhibition or co-tuning can dominate depending on input structure. Facilitating pyramid-to-GIN (non-FS) synapses are argued to contribute little to transient onsets.
ocar.future_work: Which regime dominates in vivo is left to the structure of thalamic/cortical input, not decided by this slice map alone.

summaries.beginner: In mouse auditory cortex, excitatory and inhibitory cells connect over similar short distances. Depending on the incoming pattern, that layout can either sharpen tuning or keep excitation and inhibition balanced.
summaries.intermediate: Levy and Reyes (Journal of Neuroscience, 2012) map local synaptic connectivity in the principal input layer of mouse A1 slices among pyramids, FS, and non-FS interneurons. Gaussian fits to connection probability give comparable spreads (85–114 μm). FS synapses are stronger in brief trains; synapse strength is distance-independent. Process truncation reduces connection rates but not spatial shape. The authors argue this architecture can support either lateral inhibition or co-tuning depending on input, and that facilitating non-FS (GIN) inputs are weak at stimulus onset.
summaries.advanced: Spreads are Gaussian fit parameters, not hard wiring cutoffs. “Principal input layer” is the mapped lamina; exact layer numbering should be read from the full methods. GIN/non-FS onset-quiescence is an interpretation from facilitating, initially weak EPSPs plus cited in vivo/in vitro transients. Catalog dimension is connectomics; this is slice paired recording, not volume EM.

plain_language_summary: In mouse auditory cortex, excitatory and inhibitory cells connect over similar short distances. Depending on the incoming pattern, that layout can either sharpen tuning or keep excitation and inhibition balanced.
